1001443.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from French à jour (“up to date; openwork, transparent”).
The French expression consists of à (“to, at”) and jour (“day, daylight”), literally “to the day; to daylight”.
The first element, à (“to, at”), is from Old French a (“to, towards”), from Latin ad (“to, towards, at”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“towards, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”).

en.g: a male given name from Danish Bertel

1001955.etyen:
Borrowed from Danish Bertel, a Danish form of German Berthold. The name is traditionally interpreted from Germanic elements meaning “shining” and “ruler”. First attested in the 15th century in Norway.
Compare Swedish Bertil (“male given name”).

1004003.etyen:
Uncertain. First attested in 1968. Contemporary newspaper accounts reported that the term had already been used among conscripts in the Brigaden i Nord-Norge in the 1950s, initially in the longer form Gokkoland, as a nickname for the districts around the brigade's bases in Northern Norway, especially in Indre Troms. The term was subsequently brought south into civilian usage by returning conscripts.

en.g: Blåflat; a locality in Bøverbru, Vestre Toten municipality, Innlandet, Norway, an old place traditionally associated with a pre-Christian sacrificial site
x: Blåflat på Bøverbru, nærmere himmelen kommer du ikke!

1005027.etyen: Origin uncertain. Johannes Sivesind noted that place names in Blå-/Brå- commonly develop from earlier bruar-, but considered that explanation unlikely for this hilltop site and suggested instead a connection with blote (“to hold a pagan sacrifice”), from Old Norse blóta (“to sacrifice”). Under this interpretation, the name would mean approximately “the flat where sacrifices were made”.
